extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers/writers of epic and moral prose
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic/didactic poetry and for portraying character and moral conduct in prose; includes advice on plot construction, use of tradition, imagery, dialogue, and authentic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Tradition to Authorize Fantastic Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve and incorporate the principal particulars transmitted by history or tradition (e.g., Virgil preserving prophecies, prodigies, and celebrated incidents) and use those authorities to justify parts of the poem that otherwise appear incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a fabulous or seemingly ludicrous circumstance appears in the source-tradition, retain it but qualify it in the poem so it reads naturally (examples: make the prophecy utterer plainly hungry or have a young speaker deliver a comic line). Cite or allude to tradition (Dionysius, Ovid) and, where appropriate, premise the occurrence as "appearing incredible" but warranted by tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition and Contrivance of the Fable (plot construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal beauty of an epic lies in the disposition and contrivance of the fable—how a poet expands a bare historical or scriptural outline into a full, ordered narrative rich in incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From few particulars create natural, entertaining fictions; distribute incidents so the story 'looks like a Comment upon sacred Writ' or a complete relation; ensure gradual, regular progression toward the central catastrophe (e.g., Milton's expansion of the Genesis account into Book IX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by Comparative Virtues and Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish characters by how virtues manifest: ostentation and display (equipage, address) versus substantive qualities (conduct, piety, success). Example: Turnus's ostentatious courage vs Æneas's piety and defensive courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show virtues through actions and outcomes rather than mere appearance. Let contrasts between appearance and performance reveal character (equipage may make a man 'appear more courageous', but conduct and success prove true valour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of Authorial Voice; Show Through Manners and Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong epic minimizes the poet's own intrusion and fills the work with manners, characters, and dramatized scenes; characters' speeches and soliloquies should do the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive authorial exposition. Use character-driven scenes and well-placed soliloquies (e.g., Satan's soliloquy) to convey motive and advance the fable, thereby preserving the illusion and dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of Description to Genre and Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and descriptions must match the poem's subject-matter and tone (e.g., Milton's morning description is 'wonderfully suitable to a Divine Poem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metaphors, images, and the register of language appropriate to the grandeur or divinity of the theme; avoid trivial or incongruent ornament that undermines the poem's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of Dialogue: Reasoned Moral Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues, especially on moral matters, should proceed from differences of judgment rather than heated passion, and be managed with reason and delicacy (example: Adam and Eve's dispute 'managed with Reason, not with Heat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose conversations so they reveal character and ethical stakes through reasoned argument and subtlety; avoid melodrama when a calm, rational tone better suits the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Apt and Close Similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer similes that are 'close' and apt—those that naturally illuminate the action (the serpent simile is cited as 'the closest of any in the whole Poem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select comparisons that feel natural and precisely illuminate the subject; refrain from forced or distant analogies that distract rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premising Incredible Actions; Give Reader Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recounting extraordinary or violent machines (e.g., metamorphoses), preface them by acknowledging their incredibility and supplying the context (tradition, precedent) that makes them acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's brief prefatory remark that an event 'appeared incredible, but that it was justified by Tradition' helps readers accept the marvelous and prevents gratuitous disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend Employing Classical Parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing parallels with classical masters (Homer, Ovid) both illuminates a poet's practice and 'guards against the Cavils of the Tasteless or Ignorant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical analogues to place your work in a respected lineage, to explain echoes or likenesses, and to pre-empt accusations of improper imitation or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity/Sincerity over Artifice (in voice and character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is superior to affected artifice: 'the best way in the World for a Man to seem to be any thing, is really to be what he would seem to be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters and narrator-voices authentically rather than as prolonged pretence; simulated qualities are hard to sustain and will be discovered—authenticity yields credible, durable characterization and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and Utility in Prose Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical writing skills (English letter-writing, accounts, shorthand, punctual correspondence) are of great use and should be taught and practised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers and for education: emphasize concrete correspondence exercises and concise practical prose to produce usable, clear expression rather than overvaluing classical erudition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Indiscreet Moralizing; Satirize Ostentation in Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Ostentatious or indiscreet displays of piety ('a Devotée') disparage true religion and make virtue ridiculous when presented with unseasonable moralizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting virtuous characters or preaching morality in writing, avoid constant, performative declarations of virtue; let restraint and measured action convey true goodness to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray Modesty as Root of True Courage and Magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty (as in the Spartan example) is linked with magnanimity and real courage: modest looks and behaviour reinforce moral and martial excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict modesty in characters to signal inner strength; contrast blustering external airs with genuine modesty to reveal who truly possesses magnanimity and courage.
